# Project Abstract

# **CLASP Documentation**

The CLASP platform introduces a modular, dynamic protein scaffold using rigid, synthetic  
Consensus Tetratricopeptide Repeat (CTPR) blocks to control molecular spatial distribution with  
nanometer precision \[cite: 5\]. Moving beyond traditional, constitutive scaffolds, CLASP remains  
fully inactive until a specific target or environmental cue triggers immediate assembly, offering a  
versatile, foundational chassis across biotechnology applications \[cite: 5\]. By combining an  
AI-optimized structural foundation with customizable plug-and-play modules, this project  
establishes a standardized biochemical toolkit capable of advancing non-invasive diagnostics,  
climate-resilient crop engineering, and highly efficient green energy manufacturing \[cite: 5\].

[] 

# Problems 

Here are several options, each pinpointing the field problem in one powerful statement.

\#\# Primary recommendation  
\> \*\*Life runs on proximity. Inside every cell, function emerges not merely from which proteins exist, but from when and where they come together — yet synthetic biologists can build proteins far faster than they can control how those proteins assemble, leaving the cell's most powerful layer of organization beyond deliberate design. CLASP changes this: a modular platform that lets any chosen signal command any chosen proteins to assemble, on demand, with programmable geometry — turning ind\\uced proximity from a biological accident into an engineering discipline.\*\*

\#\# Alternative 1 — problem-forward  
\> \*\*In living cells, the right molecules in the right place at the right time is the difference between health and disease, energy and waste, signal and noise. Nature controls this through induced proximity — the conditional assembly of proteins in response to a cue. But synthetic biology has mastered controlling what a cell makes, not when and how those components organize. CLASP closes that gap: a standardized platform for signal-triggered, geometrically programmable protein assembly, giving engineers command over the spatial logic that life itself depends on.\*\*

\#\# Alternative 2 — big and humanity-facing  
\> \*\*Every metabolic pathway, every diagnosis a cell makes, every molecular decision that keeps an organism alive depends on proteins finding each other at the right moment. Evolution engineers this with breathtaking precision; synthetic biologists still cannot. We can write genes, but we cannot yet direct the assembly those genes are meant to produce. CLASP makes protein assembly programmable — one signal, any payload, defined geometry — so that the tools to feed crops, detect disease, and manufacture clean energy are no longer limited by our inability to control when biology comes together.\*\*

\#\# Alternative 3 — concise and declarative  
\> \*\*Synthetic biology can control which proteins a cell produces, but not when, where, or how they assemble — and assembly is where biological function is actually decided. CLASP is a modular platform that puts protein proximity under command: a chosen signal recruits chosen payloads into a programmable arrangement, transforming induced assembly from something cells do naturally into something engineers can design deliberately.\*\*

\#\# My single strongest one-sentence version  
\> \*\*Biology's power lies not in its parts but in their assembly — and CLASP gives synthetic biologists, for the first time, a standardized way to command when, where, and how proteins come together, turning the cell's most fundamental organizing principle into programmable engineering infrastructure.\*\*  
One caution: avoid the phrase "for the first time" unless you complete a thorough prior-art review, since inducible proximity systems already exist. The defensible framing is that CLASP makes it \*\*modular, standardized, geometrically programmable, and measurable\*\* — not that induced proximity itself is new.

\# CLASP  
\#\#\# Conditional Localized Assembly of Synthetic Proteins  
\*\*Command when, where, and how proteins come together.\*\*  
\---  
Biology's power has never come from its parts alone. A cell holds thousands of proteins at once, yet it is not their mere presence that sustains life — it is their \*\*assembly\*\*. The right molecules, in the right place, at the right moment. This is how a pathway becomes efficient, how a signal becomes a decision, how raw components become function.  
Nature engineers this with extraordinary precision. In response to a cue, proteins are recruited together, do their work, and release. This conditional coming-together — induced proximity — underlies metabolism, signalling, sensing, and repair. It is one of the most fundamental organizing principles of the living world.  
Synthetic biology has learned to control what a cell produces. We can write genes, tune expression, and build entire pathways. But we have far less control over what happens next: \*\*when those proteins assemble, where they assemble, and in what arrangement.\*\* Existing protein scaffolds are largely static — permanently on, fixed in geometry, built for a single pathway, and difficult to observe or reuse. The cell's most powerful layer of organization remains, for the engineer, largely out of reach.  
\*\*CLASP closes that gap.\*\*  
CLASP is a modular platform that puts protein proximity under command. A chosen signal recruits chosen payloads onto a programmable protein scaffold, in a defined spatial arrangement, and — when needed — locks them permanently in place. Assembly is no longer constitutive; it is conditional. Geometry is no longer guessed; it is designed. And assembly itself is no longer inferred from a final product; it is measured directly, in real time.  
\---  
\#\# How it works  
\*\*A programmable scaffold.\*\* Built from consensus tetratricopeptide repeats, CLASP's backbone lets us position docking sites with nanometer-scale control over spacing and orientation.  
\*\*A signal that triggers assembly.\*\* A sensor–partner pair recruits payloads only when a chosen input is present — calcium, light, pH, or a target molecule — and releases them when it is gone.  
\*\*Any compatible payload.\*\* Sequential enzymes, recognition proteins, redox partners, and reporters. CLASP does not care what the payload does; it controls whether it assembles.  
\*\*Built-in measurement.\*\* A split-luciferase reporter turns assembly into light, so we can see whether recruitment actually happened — separately from whether the pathway worked.  
\*\*Reversible or permanent.\*\* An optional covalent lock converts a fleeting signal into a lasting molecular state.  
\---  
\#\# Why it matters  
Because the number of possible scaffold designs is far too large to test by hand, CLASP is paired with \*\*CLASP-Copilot\*\* — a design environment that models geometry, predicts performance with honest uncertainty, assembles standardized parts, and recommends the single most informative experiment to run next. Design becomes a discipline, not a guessing game.  
We demonstrate CLASP across three fundamentally different problems, each using a different form of induced proximity:  
\*\*Agriculture\*\* — clustering biosynthetic enzymes to produce protective osmolytes for crops under salt stress.  
\*\*Diagnostics\*\* — a cell-free, target-triggered assembly assay for early disease biomarkers.  
\*\*Clean energy\*\* — organizing redox partners to drive green hydrogen production.  
These are not the point. They are the proof. Any signal that can be sensed, and any proteins that function better together, are candidates for CLASP.  
\---  
With CLASP, induced proximity stops being something biology does by accident — and becomes something engineers can design on purpose. Proteins become programmable building blocks, and their assembly becomes a tool that any synthetic biologist can wield.  
\*\*CLASP — conditional protein assembly, on demand.\*\*

# Presentation

# **Complete Presentation Flow with Transitions**

The secret to coherent transitions is that **every page ends by raising a question that the next page answers**. The audience should never feel that you changed the subject. They should feel that you are following one continuous thread of logic.

The thread for CLASP is:

**Biology already controls protein assembly. We cannot yet engineer that control. CLASP builds it. ORIGAMI designs it. Every application, measurement, human practice, and sustainability decision follows from that one gap.**

## 

# **The Complete Flow**

## Opening: The Wonder

You do not open with your project name. You open with something the judge already knows is true and finds beautiful.

Every living cell already solves the problem we are trying to solve. When a signal arrives, proteins that were floating freely come together, do their work, and release — in milliseconds, without transcribing a single new gene. This conditional, spatial organization of proteins is how life achieves precision that no human engineer has yet matched. 

**Transition out:**

But here is what synthetic biology still cannot do.

## 

## Problem: The Gap

We can write genes. We can tune expressions. We can build entire metabolic pathways. But we have almost no standardized control over what happens to proteins after they are made. Existing scaffolds are permanently assembled — always on, blind to context, built for one pathway, and nearly impossible to reuse. The cell’s most powerful layer of organization — conditional, signal-responsive protein assembly — remains largely outside deliberate design

Then make it human:

That gap has a cost. A family whose crops are failing because the bacteria in the soil cannot organize the right protective molecules fast enough. A person waiting years for an Alzheimer’s diagnosis that requires a needle in their spine, when the molecular signal is already present in their saliva. A world that needs clean hydrogen but cannot yet make the biological machinery efficient enough to matter. These are not three separate problems. They are three faces of the same gap.

**Transition out:**

CLASP was built to close that gap. But before we show you what we built, we need to show you that the molecular tools we are using actually work.

## 

## Wet Lab: Proving the Hardware

Before we could build a platform, we had to prove that its individual components function as intended. We validated four fundamental molecular operations independently.

Present each operation as a named capability:

**Reversible recruitment.** Calcium activates calmodulin, which binds M13 on the scaffold. The payload arrives. When calcium falls, it releases.  
**Proximity reporting.** When the payload arrives, LgBiT and SmBiT reconstitute an active luciferase. We can see assembly happen in real time.  
**Covalent capture.** SpyTag and SpyCatcher form a permanent bond when brought into proximity. A transient signal can create a lasting molecular state.  
**Sequential catalysis.** OtsA and OtsB, organized on the scaffold, produce trehalose at a rate that exceeds the free-enzyme control.

Then show the key result:

These are not four separate experiments. They are four validated operations of one platform. Together, they prove that CLASP can recruit, report, retain, and react — on demand.

**Transition out:**

But proving that the hardware works is only the beginning. The harder question is how you design it. The number of possible scaffold geometries, payload combinations, and signal conditions is too large for exhaustive testing. We needed a way to think before we build.

## Dry Lab: The Mathematical Foundation

Before we pipetted a single experiment, we modelled it. We needed to know not just whether CLASP works, but why it works — and under what conditions it stops working.

Present the key mathematical contributions:

We modelled scaffold geometry using a CTPR structural framework, calculating docking-site coordinates, linker reach distributions, steric accessibility, and active-site orientation. We derived the Damköhler number for each candidate geometry — the ratio of reaction rate to diffusion rate — to predict whether an intermediate would be captured or lost. We used a mechanistic ODE system to model calcium activation, payload recruitment, occupancy, and reporter output. We propagated uncertainty through every prediction so that no result was presented as more precise than the evidence warranted.

Then show the prospective validation:

We froze our predictions before collecting the wet-lab results. We predicted which scaffold geometries would perform best. The wet lab tested them. The model was right about the trend. Where it was wrong, we revised it. That revision is documented. That is what an engineering cycle looks like.

**Transition out:**

The mathematics told us what to build. But mathematics alone cannot tell another team what to build for their system. We needed to turn these models into something transferable. That is what ORIGAMI does.

## Software: ORIGAMI

ORIGAMI is the mechanism-aware design engine for CLASP. It does not apply one universal proximity score to every payload. It uses a shared physical engine for scaffold geometry, linker reach, steric accessibility, and recruitment — and connects that engine to separate functional models for four distinct molecular mechanisms.

Name the four profiles:

Intermediate transfer for sequential enzymes. Target-induced complementation for cell-free detection. Redox electron transfer for biomanufacturing. Covalent capture for permanent molecular states.

Describe the three modes:

In Explore Mode, a researcher asks what evidence exists for their proposed system. ORIGAMI retrieves source passages, flags contradictions, and separates direct evidence from inference. It refuses to answer when evidence is insufficient.  
In Design Mode, a researcher specifies a biological objective and ORIGAMI converts it into a geometry, a mechanistic prediction, a standardized construct, and a verification report — with uncertainty and evidence maturity displayed at every step.  
In Learn Mode, a researcher uploads experimental results and ORIGAMI updates its model, compares prediction with observation, and recommends the next experiment.

Then make the foundational claim:

ORIGAMI does not expand by adding another prompt. It expands by adding a complete, testable mechanism profile. Every new profile must bring its own equations, controls, measurements, and validation evidence. That is how a project-specific tool becomes a field-level standard.

**Transition out:**

We built the platform. We modelled it. We built the software to design it. But a foundational advance is only foundational if it is responsible. We needed to understand who this affects, how it could be misused, and what it costs the planet to build it.

## Integrated Human Practices: Who We Listened To and What Changed

We did not treat human practices as a box to check. We treated it as a design input. Every conversation we had changed something about the project.

Structure this as a series of named conversations and their consequences:

**We spoke with farmers and agricultural scientists.** They told us that a living microbial deployment in open soil raises concerns that a laboratory proof of concept does not address. We responded by keeping the agricultural demonstration contained and by framing the platform as a tool for future responsible deployment rather than an immediate field application.  
**We spoke with clinicians and diagnostic researchers.** They told us that calling a research assay a diagnostic is dangerous. It creates false hope and can delay appropriate care. We responded by removing the word diagnostic from our primary claims and replacing it with screening-assay proof of concept.  
**We spoke with biosecurity researchers.** They told us that a modular protein-assembly platform with a software design engine raises dual-use concerns that go beyond the specific payloads we are using. We responded by building an allowlist architecture, a sequence-screening requirement, and a refusal layer into ORIGAMI.  
**We spoke with synthetic-biology students from other teams.** They told us that the most useful thing we could give them was not a better scaffold but a better design process. We responded by publishing the ORIGAMI Mechanism Profile Standard as an open protocol that any team can use to add a new proximity-dependent function.

**Transition out:**

Every conversation made the project more responsible. But responsibility is not only about who the project affects. It is also about what the project costs — in energy, in materials, in biological risk, and in the long-term consequences of releasing engineered systems into the world.

## Sustainability: What This Costs and How We Account for It

We applied a lifecycle perspective to every major decision in the project.

Present four sustainability dimensions:

**Biological burden.** Constitutively expressing a large scaffold imposes a standing metabolic cost on the host. We measured this cost and used it as a penalty term in our scaffold-optimization model. A design that improves pathway flux but severely reduces growth rate is not a net improvement.  
**Computational burden.** Every ORIGAMI query that uses a frontier language model consumes energy. We minimized this by using local embeddings, cached retrieval, deterministic sequence compilation, and lightweight statistical models. The language model is called only when retrieval alone is insufficient.  
**Chemical and material burden.** We compared containment options by their material, energy, chemical, and biological costs. We chose detergent-based lysis over sonication not only because it is more reproducible but because it reduces equipment energy consumption and operator exposure.  
**Biocontainment.** We applied our Full-Spectrum Biocontainment Assurance Standard to every application context separately. The laboratory expression host, the cell-free diagnostic format, the agricultural concept, and the biomanufacturing concept each received a separate consequence-pathway analysis, independent containment layers, and explicit evidence-maturity ratings.

Then make the sustainability claim:

Sustainability is not a section of our project. It is a design constraint that shaped every decision from scaffold length to software architecture.

**Transition out:**

We have shown you the problem, the hardware, the mathematics, the software, the human conversations that shaped it, and the sustainability decisions that constrained it. There is one more thing a foundational advance must do. It must teach.

## Education: Making the Knowledge Transferable

A platform that only experts can use is not a platform. It is a demonstration. We built three educational contributions to make CLASP and ORIGAMI accessible beyond our team.

Present three named contributions:

**The CLASP Design Standard.** A modular manual that tells any team how to translate a biological objective into a compatible CLASP design, model it, build it, test it, and decide whether it worked. It covers sequential enzymes, kinase–substrate systems, split reporters, covalent capture, and other proximity-dependent mechanisms. It is published openly and written for a team that has never heard of CTPR.  
**The ORIGAMI Mechanism Profile Standard.** A protocol for adding a new proximity-dependent function to ORIGAMI. Any team can contribute a new profile by supplying the biological objective, governing equations, required controls, validation requirements, and evidence maturity. The standard ensures that ORIGAMI grows without sacrificing scientific rigor.  
**The Proximity Design Passport.** A standardized output document that any team can generate from ORIGAMI and submit alongside their ISEF project. It records the mechanism, geometry, parameters, predictions, uncertainty, controls, measurements, and evidence maturity of any CLASP-based design. It is the design record that makes results reproducible and comparable across teams.

Then make the education claim:

We are not asking other teams to trust our results. We are giving them the tools to generate their own — and to contribute back to a shared design space that makes every future team’s work easier.

**Transition out:**

We began with a gap between what biology does and what engineers can design. We close with a platform, a software engine, a design standard, a measurement framework, a biocontainment architecture, and an open invitation to build on what we started.

## Closing: The Invitation

CLASP is not finished. It is a foundation. Every team that uses it contributes to a shared design space. Every experiment that enters ORIGAMI makes the next prediction more accurate. Every new payload that is validated expands what the platform can do.

Then return to the opening image:

We began by describing what every living cell already does — assembling the right proteins in the right place at the right moment, in response to a signal, without waiting for new genes to be written. That capability has existed in biology for billions of years. CLASP gives synthetic biologists the same power — on demand, with any signal, for any payload, in any organism.

Then your final line:

That is not one application. That is a new layer of biological control. And it belongs to everyone.

## One Rule for Every Transition

Every transition should follow this template:

**\[What we just showed you\] is necessary but not sufficient. The harder question is \[what comes next\]. That is what \[next section\] addresses.**

Examples:

“Proving that the hardware works is necessary but not sufficient. The harder question is how you design it. That is what the dry lab addresses.”  
“The mathematics told us what to build, but mathematics alone is not transferable to another team. The harder question is how you make the design process reusable. That is what ORIGAMI addresses.”  
“A powerful tool must be a responsible one. The harder question is who it affects and how it could be misused. That is what our human practices work addresses.”  
“Responsibility is not only about who the project affects. It is also about what it costs. The harder question is whether the project is sustainable. That is what our lifecycle analysis addresses.”  
“A foundational advance is only foundational if other teams can use it. The harder question is how you make the knowledge transferable. That is what our education work addresses.”

If you use that template for every transition, the presentation will feel like one continuous argument rather than a collection of separate sections.

## The Single Most Important Structural Decision

Do not present the three applications as three separate stories. Present them as **one story with three demonstrations**.

The story is: the gap between natural and engineered protein assembly has a human cost across multiple domains.

The demonstrations are: agriculture, diagnostics, and hydrogen show that the same platform can address that cost in three fundamentally different ways.

If you present them as three separate stories, the judge will ask: “Which one is your real project?”

If you present them as one story with three demonstrations, the judge will understand: “This is a platform, not a product.”

That distinction is the difference between a good project and a foundational advance.

# Description

# **Conditional Localized Assembly of Synthetic Proteins**

##  Building Molecular Assembly Lines That Turn On Only When You Want Them To

## **🌟 Overview**

**CLASP** stands for **Conditional Localized Assembly of Synthetic Proteins**. 

Living cells are full of tiny protein machines called **enzymes.** These are the workers that build and break down molecules to keep life running. **CLASP** is a system that grabs a group of enzymes and lines them up in close proximity *only when a specific signal appears*. When they're lined up, they work much faster. When the signal goes away, they can optionally drift apart again. It's an on-demand production line, built at the scale of molecules. 


*Scaffy \- a mascot of a protein scaffold that I generated in NanoBanana.* 

## **🤔 Why Would Enzymes Need Help Lining Up?**

Here's the thing: most enzymes just float around loose inside a cell, bumping into their ingredients by random chance. Imagine a factory where every worker wanders around the whole building hoping to accidentally run into the next worker. Stuff still gets made — just slowly.


Cells actually discovered a fix a long time ago. Sometimes they clip enzymes together into a cluster so the product made by enzyme \#1 gets handed *directly* to enzyme \#2, without floating away and getting lost. Scientists call this **substrate channelling** (a "substrate" is just the ingredient an enzyme works on). It's a bit like passing a bucket of water hand-to-hand instead of everyone running to the well individually. 

Scientists have copied this trick before by building **scaffolds** — structures that hold enzymes in place. But those older scaffolds had a catch: they were **always on**. Once built, they stayed clustered permanently, whether the cell needed the boost or not.

**CLASP's new twist:** our scaffold stays switched *off* until a signal tells it to switch *on*. That's the whole innovation. 

## 

## **🧩 The Three Building Blocks**

CLASP is made of three parts that snap together. We designed all of them as standardized, swappable pieces (more on that later), so you can mix and match like modular building blocks.

### **Part A — The Scaffold 🪜** 

The scaffold is a long, stiff protein made from repeating units called **CTPR** (Consensus Tetratricopeptide Repeat — quite a mouthful, so we'll just say CTPR). Each unit is a small, sturdy coil, and you stack them like identical bricks. The more bricks you add, the longer the scaffold — and because the length is so predictable, we can control *exactly* how far apart the enzymes sit. Spacing matters a lot for teamwork, so being able to dial it in precisely is a big deal. 

![][image3]

Along the scaffold, at spots we choose, we add little grabbing hooks called **docking sites** where enzymes can attach.

### 

### **Part B — The Signal Sensor 🚦**

This is the part that decides *when* assembly happens. It's a pair of proteins that only stick together when a specific signal is present. Think of it as a lock that opens only for the right key.

We built a whole menu of sensors so you can pick your trigger:

Signal you want to detect : **Calcium** (Ca²⁺, an ion cells use for messaging)   
What responds to it : **Calmodulin** grabbing a partner peptide  
What Calmodulin binds to : **M13**  high affinity peptide that gets bound to calmodulin.  
![][image4]  
Other than calcium ions only, this system is built to work with other signals. For example, **Blue light** (Proteins that clump together when blue light is present)**, Acidity**(Proteins that clump together when pH reaches/drops below a certain threshold), or **Temperature** (Proteins that clump above a set temperature).

This allows us to be universal, modular, and portable across domains. 

The clever part: one half of the pair sits on the scaffold, and the other half is attached to the enzyme. No signal → they ignore each other. Signal present → they lock together, and the enzyme gets pulled onto the scaffold. 

This binding not only signals the presence of calcium ions (or whatever signal you choose), it would also be the main driving force for the two payloads to go near each other due to the signal-responsive proteins’ high affinity binding (between Calmodulin and M13 in this case). This singlehandedly allows the binding of SpyCatcher/SpyTag and LgBiT/SmBiT, now that they are in close proximity. 

### 

### 

### **Part C — The Enzyme Payload 🔧** 

This is whatever enzyme *you* want to speed up. We attach it to its sensor half using a flexible connector (so it can wiggle into position), and it's completely plug-and-play. The user of the system can just swap in any enzyme you like for whatever job you're doing.

![][image5]

In the calcium model, the enzymes in question are OtsA and OtsB, for the final product of trehalose. The enzymes perform their actions much much quicker because they undergo substrate channeling in enzyme clustering. 

## 

## **⚙️ How It All Comes Together, Step by Step**

Let's walk through it using **calcium** as the example signal:

1. **OFF state 😴** : Calcium is low. The sensor pair ignores each other. Enzymes float around loose and slow.  
2. **Signal arrives ⚡** : Calcium levels rise. The calcium-sensing protein changes shape, revealing a sticky pocket.  
3. **Assembly\! 🧲** : That sticky pocket grabs its partner on the scaffold. The enzyme is now pulled into place. If several enzymes get recruited, they end up neighbors, assembly lines formed.  
4. **Speed boost 🚀** : Because the enzymes are packed close, products get handed straight down the line (that's the **substrate channelling** from earlier). The whole process speeds up dramatically.  
5. **Signal leaves 🌙**: Calcium drops, the sensor lets go, and the enzymes drift apart again. Back to the OFF state.

## 

## **💡 The Built-In Reporter**

How do you *know*, from the outside, that all these invisible molecules actually assembled? We gave CLASP a built-in glow. ✨

We use a glowing protein called **luciferase** (the same family of chemistry that makes fireflies light up ), but split into two halves. One half rides on the scaffold, the other rides on the enzyme. On their own, both halves are dark. But when assembly happens and they're brought together, the two halves reunite into a working, glowing luciferase.


**More assembly \= more glow.** So the brightness is a live, real-time meter of how well the system is working. This lets us measure everything precisely and test thousands of designs quickly. 

## 

## **🔒 Bonus Mode: The Permanent Lock**

Sometimes you don't want the enzymes to drift apart when the signal fades — you want them stuck together for good. For those cases, we added an optional **snap-lock**: a pair of parts called **SpyTag** and **SpyCatcher** that form a permanent chemical bond the moment they're pushed close together. 


SpyTag and SpyCatcher spontaneously form an irreversible isopeptide bond when brought into close proximity. 

The reaction occurs between the side‑chain amine of a lysine (K31) in SpyCatcher and the side‑chain carboxyl of an aspartate (D117) in SpyTag, creating a covalent amide linkage without any external energy or cofactors. This bond is stable under denaturing conditions (heat, SDS, urea) and permanently locks the two proteins together.

Once locked, the assembly stays put even after the signal disappears. You choose reversible or permanent depending on your project. 🎛️

So, what would the final construct look like? 


The construct is split into two parts in total. As we discussed, the two payloads are formed by the three parts above: scaffold, signal, enzyme. 

The first model in the image is the scaffold construct. It consists of the **receptor proteins** attached on a rod of rigid CTPR (5 in total to ensure close proximity). The receptor proteins are derived from the two docking stations (SpyCatcher, LgBiT), and the signal-responsive protein  (M13).

The second model in the image is the enzyme construct. It consists of the **ligand proteins** on the enzyme (SpyTag, SmBiT), attached to the signal-responsive protein (Calmodulin). The model above shows it in its **inactivated** state, where no signal is present yet to activate the signal-responsive payloads. 

The final model in the image shows the **activated** state, where calcium ions are finally present and bind to Calmodulin on the enzyme payload. The final image shows the sequence of bindings finally happening in the following order: Calmodulin+M13 (bind due to high affinity), SpyCatcher+SpyTag (bind due to close proximity with each other), and LgBiT+SmBiT (bind due to close proximity with each other). The visible cue we get from the sequence of events to indicate success is the glowing part produced by the binding of LgBiT and SmBiT. 

To facilitate enzyme clustering, we need to attach 2 enzyme payloads to the same scaffold. In the context of calcium ions, and trehalose production, those two enzymes would be defined as OtsA and OtsB.

## **🌍 Three Real-World Problems CLASP Could Help Solve**

CLASP isn't built for just one job, it's more of a toolkit. Here are three very different demonstrations of what it can do:

### 🧠 **Healthcare — An Early, Painless Alzheimer's Test**

Alzheimer's disease is easier to manage when caught early, but today's tests are expensive or invasive (think spinal taps and pricey brain scans). Certain warning-sign molecules show up in **saliva**. We designed a spit-based version of CLASP that lights up when those molecules are present: a cheap, painless, "mix-and-read" screening test. (It would still need a doctor's confirmation, do view it more as an early warning, not a final diagnosis.) 

### **🌾 Agriculture — Crops That Survive Salty Soil**

Salty soil ruins huge amounts of farmland and starves crops. We put CLASP into a helpful root bacterium. When the plant hits salt stress, calcium rises, CLASP assembles, and it cranks out **trehalose**, which is a natural protective sugar right at the root where it's needed most. Healthier roots, tougher plants. 

### 🔋 **Green Energy — Clean Hydrogen Fuel from Light**

Hydrogen is a clean fuel, but most of it is made from fossil fuels today. We used the **blue-light** version of CLASP to line up hydrogen-producing enzymes. Shine blue light→ enzymes assemble → hydrogen gets made. Turn the light off → production stops. Fuel on demand, powered by light. 

## **🤖 The Sidekick Software: CLASP-Copilot**

Designing biology by hand is slow, so we also built a smart assistant. You ask a plain-English question like *"I want to cluster these enzymes, triggered by acidity, in yeast — what should I build?"* and it:

* 🔎 **Looks up** past results and published science to give you an evidence-backed answer  
* 📈 **Predicts** how well a design will work before you build it  
* 🧾 **Writes the DNA blueprint** ready to order  
* 🔁 **Suggests the next experiment** to run, learning from every result you feed back in

The more people use it, the smarter it gets — every experiment makes the whole community's toolkit better. 🌐

## 

## **🧱 The Secret Sauce: Everything Is Standardized**

Here's what ties it all together. Every CLASP part is built to the same connection standard (a lab method called **Golden Gate / MoClo assembly**), which means swapping any piece: a new sensor, a new enzyme, a new glowing reporter is a quick, single-tube reaction. 

Because the parts behave the same way regardless of the host, the same CLASP system can work in bacteria, yeast, or human cells with only small tweaks. That's what makes it a genuine *platform* rather than a one-off gadget.

## **🎯 So, Back to That Name**

**CLASP \= Conditional Localized Assembly of Synthetic Proteins**

* **Conditional** → it only turns on when the right signal shows up   
* **Localized** → it brings enzymes together in one precise spot   
* **Assembly** → it builds a working molecular team   
* **Synthetic Proteins** → all from parts we designed and can customize 

Put simply: **CLASP is a signal-controlled "on switch" for molecular teamwork**, and because every piece is swappable, it's less like a single invention and more like a whole new set of building blocks for biology. 

Link to the AI explainer video: [https://youtu.be/dxkiJFZz1zE?si=iK3IUNfiFPyHZDeq](https://youtu.be/dxkiJFZz1zE?si=iK3IUNfiFPyHZDeq) 

# Concepts

# **CLASP Initial Developments**

## **1\. The Core Concept**

CLASP uses a **synthetic protein scaffold** that stays inactive until a **user‑chosen signal** (calcium, light, pH…) arrives. That signal triggers physical recruitment of any enzymes you've tagged onto the scaffold, clustering them so they work many times faster. A built-in light reporter shows you it's working in real time.

## **2\. The Three Standardised Parts**

Every part is stored in Level 0 Modular Cloning vectors with standardised 4‑bp fusion sites, so you can mix & match them in one‑pot reactions.

### **Part A – The Universal Scaffold Backbone**

* **Protein:** Consensus Tetratricopeptide Repeat (CTPR) arrays.  
* **Why CTPR:** These are rigid, superhelical helix‑turn‑helix repeats. You can precisely program their length (number of repeats) and thus the spacing between enzyme binding sites.  
* **Modification:** At defined positions along the CTPR array, we insert **M13 peptides** (or other “acceptor” dimerisation motifs) via loop grafting.  
* **Cloning:** The array is built by hierarchical Golden Gate from repeat units; different spacings (e.g., every 2nd, 3rd repeat) create a library of scaffold geometries.  
* **Optional:** For irreversible locking, some positions carry a **SpyCatcher domain** instead of M13. A mixed scaffold (M13 \+ SpyCatcher) enables both recruitment and covalent capture.

### 

### **Part B – The Signal‑Responsive Recruitment Module**

This is a pair of proteins that bind each other **only** when the signal is present.

| Sensor | Dimerisation Pair | Mechanism |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Calcium (Ca²⁺) | Calmodulin (CaM) \+ M13 peptide | Ca²⁺ binding to CaM exposes a hydrophobic pocket that grabs the M13 helix |
| Blue light | pMag \+ nMag (from *Arabidopsis* cryptochrome) | Light induces homodimerisation of the photosensory domain; pMag/nMag are complementary engineered magnets |
| Low pH (acid) | Acid‑stable coiled‑coil pair (e.g., from vulture stomach *Peptostreptococcus*) | Protonation of glutamate residues triggers folding and heterodimerisation |
| Temperature | Elastin‑like polypeptide (ELP) \+ ELP‑binding domain | Above a tunable transition temperature, ELPs aggregate and capture a fused binding partner |

One half of the pair is fused to the **scaffold** (e.g., M13 peptide already in the scaffold, or a coiled‑coil grafted onto a CTPR loop). The other half is fused to the **enzyme** payload.

### **Part C – The Enzyme Payload (Plug‑and‑Play)**

Any enzyme of interest is expressed as a fusion: \[Signal‑responsive partner\] – \[flexible linker\] – \[Enzyme\] – \[optional SpyTag\]

* The signal‑responsive partner (e.g., Calmodulin, pMag, acid‑coil) directs the enzyme to the scaffold when the signal is present.  
* The optional SpyTag at the C‑terminus (or a separate SpyTag fusion) can be placed so that once the enzyme is recruited, SpyTag and SpyCatcher are close enough to react covalently and lock the assembly permanently. This is useful for pathways where you want a one‑time, irreversible boost.

## 

## **3\. The Assembly Mechanism – Two Modes**

**Mode 1: Reversible clusters**

Scaffold‑M13 fusion and Enzyme‑CaM fusion are constitutively expressed at low levels.

1. In the **absence** of Ca²⁺, CaM does not bind M13; enzymes float freely.  
2. When Ca²⁺ rises (e.g., via CAX1 activity), CaM grabs M13, co‑localising the enzyme onto the scaffold.  
3. When Ca²⁺ drops, they dissociate.

**Mode 2: Irreversible clusters**

1. The scaffold carries a SpyCatcher adjacent to the M13 peptide.  
2. The enzyme fusion contains both CaM and SpyTag, with a flexible linker that allows the SpyTag to reach the SpyCatcher only when CaM is bound to M13.  
3. Ca²⁺ → CaM‑M13 binding → SpyTag and SpyCatcher are forced into proximity → spontaneous covalent isopeptide bond forms.  
4. Even after Ca²⁺ disappears, the enzyme is permanently anchored.

Both modes are available in the part library; users choose based on their application.

## **4\. Built‑in Real‑Time Reporter (Split Luciferase)**

To see assembly instantly and enable high‑throughput screening, we embed a reporter:

* The scaffold carries the **large fragment of NanoLuc** (LgBiT).  
* A “dummy” protein (or an enzyme) carries the **small fragment** (SmBiT, 11 amino acids) along with the recruitment domain.  
* When scaffold and payload come together, LgBiT and SmBiT reconstitute an active luciferase → bright luminescence proportional to assembly efficiency.

This readout is:

* **Quantitative:** Measure luminescence in a plate reader to get dose‑response curves (vary Ca²⁺ concentration, light intensity, pH).  
* **Sortable:** Use FACS on cells expressing GFP instead of luciferase (or a coupled operon) to screen millions of scaffold variants.  
* **Sequenceable:** Sort “bright” and “dim” populations, amplify the scaffold region, and use NGS to map which scaffold geometry (repeat number, M13/SpyCatcher placement) gives the best assembly for a given enzyme set.

## **5\. The Engineering Pipeline – From Idea to Validated Part**

### **Step 1: Scaffold Geometry Library Construction**

* Synthesise a “parent” CTPR array of, say, 10 repeats with unique restriction sites at loop positions.  
* Use Golden Gate to insert M13 peptides and SpyCatcher domains in different patterns (e.g., every repeat, every 2nd, 3rd, etc.).  
* Clone each variant into an expression plasmid with a constitutive promoter and the LgBiT fragment.

### **Step 2: Enzyme Payload Library**

* Fuse Calmodulin (or other sensor partner) \+ enzyme \+ SpyTag \+ SmBiT via flexible (GGGGS)₃ linkers.  
* Ensure the fusion is tested for enzyme activity; activity assays (colorimetric, HPLC) confirm that tagging doesn't kill the enzyme.

### **Step 3: Co‑expression and Dose‑Response Testing**

* Co‑transform E. coli with scaffold variant \+ enzyme payload.  
* Induce with IPTG (low level) to express both, then apply a gradient of the signal (Ca²⁺ concentration in medium, light intensity, pH‑buffered media).  
* Measure luminescence over time → build **transfer functions** (luminescence vs. signal strength) for every scaffold geometry.

### **Step 4: High‑Throughput Screening & “Winner Cluster” Dictionary**

* Create a pooled library of 10⁵ scaffold variants (randomised spacing, number of binding sites) and a single enzyme pair.  
* Subject the pool to a chosen signal level, sort top 1% brightest cells by FACS, and sequence the scaffold region.  
* For each unique sequence, compute an Assembly Efficiency Score (AES \= luminescence per OD per enzyme concentration).  
* Store all results in an open **Dictionary of Clusters** — a website where a user can input their desired signal type and enzyme pathway, and the software recommends the optimal scaffold geometry with highest recorded AES.

### **Step 5: Portability Validation (The Grand Prize Data)**

* Take the top 3 scaffold‑payload combinations from E. coli and re‑synthesise them with chassis‑appropriate promoters for:  
  * *E coli.* (your salt‑stress application)  
  * *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* (yeast, for ethanol‑triggered systems)  
  * HEK293 mammalian cells (for a therapeutic demo)  
* Show that the assembly transfer function (luminescence vs. signal) remains essentially identical across all four organisms, proving platform universality.

## **6\. How Your Agriculture Application Fits (One of Many Demos)**

Your existing HKT1/CAX1 system becomes the **I‑SENSE module** that generates a Ca²⁺ signal. The CLASP scaffold (CaM‑M13 type) loaded with trehalose‑synthesising enzymes is expressed in *B. subtilis* biofilm. When salt stress activates CAX1 and HKT1, Ca²⁺ rises, scaffold assembles, trehalose is made exactly at the root surface, and the root glows (via luciferase) to show protection. The farmer sees nothing but healthy plants; the lab sees quantitative, transferable assembly.

## 

## **7\. The Software Tool: AI‑Powered Design Engine for the CLASP Platform**

The software behind CLASP is not a simple calculator—it’s a **retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) system** with an integrated **active‑learning machine‑learning (ML) core** that serves as a full‑stack bio‑design assistant. It answers questions, predicts performance, generates parts, and learns from every new experiment. Here’s what it can do:

### **1\. Intelligent Query & Retrieval**

* Users ask natural language questions: *“I want to cluster three enzymes for menthol biosynthesis in yeast, triggered by low pH. What scaffold geometry should I use?”*  
* The RAG engine retrieves relevant information from:  
  * The CLASP **Dictionary of Clusters** (thousands of characterized (scaffold × sensor × enzyme) combinations with measured Assembly Efficiency Scores, AES).  
  * The ISEF Registry and literature (via PubMed/arXiv embeddings).  
  * The team’s own lab‑notebook data and modelling logs.  
* It then uses a large language model (LLM) to synthesise a context‑rich answer with citations, showing proven designs, potential pitfalls, and adaptation notes.

### **2\. Predictive Performance Modelling**

* An ensemble of **gradient‑boosted trees and graph neural networks** trained on FACS‑seq and plate‑reader data predicts AES for any user‑defined scaffold–sensor–enzyme combination.  
* Input features include:  
  * Scaffold: CTPR repeat number, binding‑site spacing, SpyCatcher vs. M13 ratio.  
  * Sensor: Ca²⁺ affinity of Calmodulin variant, light‑intensity half‑max, pH‑coil transition midpoint.  
  * Enzymes: size, pI, predicted diffusion coefficient, kinetic parameters (kcat, Km).  
  * Chassis: growth temperature, intracellular crowding, orthogonal copy number.  
* The model outputs a **predicted flux increase** for the desired pathway, along with uncertainty intervals.

### **3\. Generative Sequence Design**

* The system can **de novo design** a complete DNA sequence for the scaffold, sensor fusions, and enzyme payloads, optimized for the chosen chassis.  
* Uses a constrained transformer model that:  
  * Compiles Golden Gate‑compatible MoClo parts from the user’s specification.  
  * Inserts the correct fusion linkers (GGGGS₃, rigid helical linkers) with predicted flexibility.  
  * Codon‑optimises the entire operon for *E. coli*, *B. subtilis*, *S. cerevisiae*, or human cells.  
  * Ensures no forbidden restriction sites are present.  
* Outputs a GenBank file and a shopping list of primers/parts, ready for synthesis.

### **4\. Active Learning & Experiment Scheduler**

* Once a user builds and tests a CLASP circuit, they upload their AES measurement.  
* The system uses **Bayesian optimization** to suggest the next round of scaffold variants that will most improve the model’s certainty and push the performance frontier.  
* It can recommend a minimal set of experiments—for example, “Test the 4‑repeat scaffold with M13 at positions 2 and 4, and a medium‑strength promoter”—that maximises information gain.

### **5\. Cross‑Chassis Portability Advisor**

* Users often want to move a working CLASP system from *E. coli* to another organism.  
* The RAG module collects all known expression context data (promoter strengths, RBS efficiency, codon usage tables, intracellular ion concentrations) for the target chassis.  
* The ML layer predicts how the transfer function (luminescence vs. signal) will shift, then the generative designer adjusts linkers, degradation tags, or promoters to compensate.  
* This turns a process that usually takes months into a single afternoon of in‑silico refinement.

### **6\. Database and Community Growth**

* Every successful design is automatically added to the **Dictionary of Clusters** with DOIs and contributor credits.  
* Researchers worldwide can query, contribute, and benchmark their own data against the platform.  
* The LLM can be prompted to write entire “Methods” sections or suggest follow‑up experiments, acting as a permanent collaborator.

### **Why This is a Winning ISEF Software Component**

* **Closed loop**: Combines high‑throughput data → AI model → generative design → experimental validation → active learning → improved model.  
* **Truly foundational**: Other teams can use CLASP‑Copilot for their own projects, even if they never build a scaffold themselves. It becomes the standard interface for dynamic enzyme clustering.  
* **RAG makes it “alive”**: Judges see that the tool doesn’t just crunch numbers; it reads and reasons over the team’s own characterisation data and the whole of synthetic biology literature, just like a human expert.

In essence, CLASP‑Copilot turns your project into a **self‑improving, AI‑driven platform** where every experiment makes the entire field smarter—exactly the type of software that defines a Grand Prize foundational advance.

## 

## **In Summary**

CLASP is engineered from:

**(1)** a rigid, programmable CTPR scaffold with signal‑responsive docking peptides,

**(2)** a library of plug‑in sensor dimerisers (CaM‑M13, pMag‑nMag, acid‑coils),

**(3)** enzyme‑partner fusions that carry a built‑in split‑luciferase reporter,

**(4)** a Golden Gate assembly standard that makes swapping any component a single‑tube reaction, and

**(5)** a high‑throughput screening pipeline that generates a transferable “Dictionary of Clusters” so any researcher can instantly deploy this system in their organism of choice.
