# Biosecurity essay

\# Proposed framework name  
\#\# \*\*Full-Spectrum Biocontainment Assurande Standard\*\*  
This is intentionally a descriptive technical name rather than another acronym. It communicates the framework’s central principle:  
\> \*\*Biocontainment is not a single kill switch. It is a lifecycle-wide assurance system in which independent physical, biological, ecological, informational, and governance controls are selected from an explicit risk model, quantitatively tested, and continuously re-evaluated.\*\*  
The framework should be presented as a \*\*proposed standardized method\*\*, not automatically as the world’s first or a proven revolution. Its genuine contribution would be integrating existing good practices into a modular, measurable, project-independent design process.  
\---  
\# What the framework is  
Most student projects discuss biocontainment by naming one control—for example, an auxotrophy, inducible kill switch, laboratory containment level, or environmental dependency—and treating that control as sufficient.  
That approach has three weaknesses.  
First, every containment mechanism has failure modes. A genetic kill switch can mutate, become inactive, impose a fitness cost, or behave differently outside laboratory conditions. An auxotrophy can fail if the required metabolite exists in the environment or is supplied by another organism. Physical containment can fail through spills, waste handling, transport, equipment failure, or human error.  
Second, the containment design is often disconnected from the project lifecycle. Teams focus on the engineered organism but pay less attention to DNA storage, culture transport, experimental waste, software access, device disposal, product purification, scale-up, or future deployment.  
Third, containment is often described qualitatively. Terms such as “safe,” “unlikely to escape,” and “cannot survive outside the laboratory” are used without a measurable performance requirement.  
The proposed architecture replaces that single-mechanism mindset with \*\*defense in depth\*\*. Every project is assessed across its entire lifecycle, and every important failure pathway is assigned multiple independent controls.  
This aligns with the WHO’s risk- and evidence-based approach to biosafety and biosecurity, ISO 35001’s process of identifying, assessing, controlling, and monitoring biological risk, and the NIH Guidelines’ assignment of explicit institutional and investigator responsibilities. (\[iso.org\](https://www.iso.org/standard/71293.html?utm\_source=openai))  
\---  
\# Why it is potentially important  
The framework’s strongest contribution is not inventing another kill switch. It is turning biocontainment into a \*\*standardized engineering discipline\*\*.  
It changes the design question from:  
\> “What containment mechanism should we add?”  
to:  
\> “What are the credible routes from our system to harm, which independent barriers interrupt each route, how will we test those barriers, and what happens when one of them fails?”  
That is a major conceptual improvement because it treats containment as a system property rather than a genetic part.  
The framework is also designed to be transferable. A team working on a bacterial agricultural product, a cell-free diagnostic, a bioreactor, an engineered yeast, or a protein-only product would use the same decision process but select different controls.  
Its most distinctive features should be:  
\- \*\*Lifecycle scope:\*\* from design and procurement through experimentation, storage, transport, waste, scale-up, deployment, and end-of-life.  
\- \*\*Consequence-first assessment:\*\* begin with credible harms, not only with a list of organisms.  
\- \*\*Independent containment layers:\*\* avoid relying on several controls that share the same failure mode.  
\- \*\*Quantitative acceptance criteria:\*\* containment claims require measurable thresholds.  
\- \*\*Evidence maturity levels:\*\* separate theoretical controls from experimentally tested and independently reproduced controls.  
\- \*\*Sustainability integration:\*\* evaluate whether a containment mechanism increases energy, material, chemical, or waste burdens.  
\- \*\*Human and organizational controls:\*\* recognize that training, documentation, access, review, and incident response are part of containment.  
\- \*\*Graceful failure:\*\* define what the system does when evidence is missing or a control fails.  
WHO’s 2024 biosecurity guidance similarly emphasizes consequence-driven risk assessment across the value chain, including emerging technologies, information security, institutional oversight, and lifecycle management. (\[who.int\](https://www.who.int/publications/b/69836?utm\_source=openai))  
\---  
\# The framework  
\#\# 1\. Define the system boundary  
Every assessment begins by defining exactly what is being contained.  
The project must identify:  
\- The organism or cell-free system  
\- Recombinant DNA and plasmids  
\- Expressed proteins and metabolites  
\- Selectable markers  
\- Mobile genetic elements  
\- Culture volumes  
\- Laboratory procedures  
\- Equipment  
\- Waste streams  
\- Software-generated sequences  
\- Intended product  
\- Intended environment of use  
\- Likely users  
\- End-of-life pathway  
This prevents teams from discussing only the engineered cell while ignoring the DNA, product, waste, device, or information associated with it.  
For CLASP, the boundary should distinguish at least four entities:  
1\. The laboratory expression host    
2\. The CLASP genetic constructs    
3\. The purified scaffold or reporter product    
4\. Any proposed future application system    
A cell-free Alzheimer’s screening assay, for example, has a fundamentally different containment profile from a living root-associated bacterium. They should not receive the same assessment merely because they share molecular components.  
\---  
\#\# 2\. Establish the intended operating envelope  
The operating envelope defines the conditions under which the system is intended to function.  
It should include:  
\- Host organism  
\- Temperature range  
\- Nutrient conditions  
\- pH  
\- Salinity  
\- Oxygen status  
\- Required inducers  
\- Required cofactors  
\- Physical location  
\- Culture volume  
\- Intended duration  
\- Approved operators  
\- Approved equipment  
\- Permitted transport and storage conditions  
Anything outside this envelope is treated as an off-normal condition requiring separate evaluation.  
For example, a system characterized in purified lysate cannot automatically be described as safe or functional in soil. A construct characterized in \*E. coli\* cannot automatically be assumed to behave similarly in \*Bacillus subtilis\*. The framework therefore treats changes in chassis, environment, scale, or application as a \*\*new containment context\*\*, not a routine extension.  
\---  
\#\# 3\. Construct consequence pathways  
Rather than beginning with a preferred kill switch, the team identifies credible chains of events that could lead to harm.  
A consequence pathway can be represented as:  
\\\[  
\\text{Initiating event}  
\\rightarrow  
\\text{containment breach}  
\\rightarrow  
\\text{survival or persistence}  
\\rightarrow  
\\text{exposure}  
\\rightarrow  
\\text{harm}  
\\\]  
Examples of initiating events include:  
\- Accidental spill  
\- Incorrect waste disposal  
\- Equipment failure  
\- Mislabelling  
\- Unauthorized access  
\- Sample transport failure  
\- Genetic mutation  
\- Horizontal gene transfer  
\- Human procedural error  
\- Software-generated inappropriate construct  
\- Scale-up beyond validated conditions  
The assessment must distinguish between:  
\- \*\*Hazard:\*\* the system’s potential to cause harm  
\- \*\*Exposure:\*\* whether a person or environment encounters it  
\- \*\*Persistence:\*\* whether it survives or remains active  
\- \*\*Consequence:\*\* the severity of the resulting effect  
\- \*\*Uncertainty:\*\* how well these factors are known  
The risk estimate should not be treated as a precise universal number. A simple semi-quantitative formulation is:  
\\\[  
R\_i \= P\_i \\times C\_i \\times U\_i  
\\\]  
where \\(P\_i\\) is the estimated likelihood of pathway \\(i\\), \\(C\_i\\) is its consequence severity, and \\(U\_i\\) is an uncertainty multiplier or uncertainty category.  
A high-uncertainty pathway should not be interpreted as low risk merely because no incidents have been observed.  
\---  
\#\# 4\. Design independent containment layers  
Each significant pathway should be interrupted by more than one control, preferably using controls with different physical or organizational failure modes.  
\#\#\# Physical containment  
This includes:  
\- Appropriate laboratory containment  
\- Closed vessels  
\- Secondary containment  
\- Controlled storage  
\- Access restriction  
\- Validated decontamination  
\- Spill-response procedures  
\- Waste segregation  
\- Transport packaging  
Physical containment remains the first layer for laboratory research. Biological containment should complement it, not be used as a reason to weaken it.  
\#\#\# Genetic containment  
This can include:  
\- Reduced environmental fitness  
\- Dependency on a controlled nutrient  
\- Dependency on a synthetic metabolite  
\- Conditional viability  
\- Removal of unnecessary mobile elements  
\- Reduced plasmid persistence  
\- Genetic isolation strategies  
\- Programmed loss of function  
No genetic mechanism should be described as escape-proof. Genetic controls require mutation, evolutionary-stability, and environmental-rescue testing before strong claims are made.  
\#\#\# Functional containment  
Functional containment limits what the engineered system can do even if some material escapes.  
Examples include:  
\- Non-replicating cell-free formats  
\- Purified protein rather than living-cell deployment  
\- Inactive precursors  
\- Restricted payload allowlists  
\- Removal of unnecessary biological functions  
\- Separation of sensing and execution components  
\- Dependence on externally supplied reaction components  
For CLASP, moving a diagnostic from living-cell operation to a purified, cell-free format is not simply a usability decision. It substantially changes the containment profile by removing organism replication from the application.  
\#\#\# Ecological containment  
Ecological containment asks whether the system can persist, reproduce, spread, transfer genes, or obtain required resources outside its intended environment.  
The assessment should examine:  
\- Environmental availability of required nutrients  
\- Potential metabolic cross-feeding  
\- Competitors and predators  
\- Temperature and pH tolerance  
\- Persistence in water or soil  
\- Biofilm formation  
\- Horizontal gene-transfer routes  
\- Selection pressure maintaining the construct  
\- Reversibility after an unintended release  
The team should not claim that an organism “cannot survive outside its niche” without testing or strong evidence.  
\#\#\# Informational containment  
Modern biocontainment also concerns data, sequence access, and software.  
Controls can include:  
\- Restricted access to sensitive construct records  
\- Role-based permissions  
\- Sequence screening before export  
\- Approved-parts libraries  
\- Audit logs  
\- Version control  
\- Refusal of hazardous software requests  
\- Separation of public design guidance from executable sensitive outputs  
\- Secure handling of API credentials and experimental records  
WHO’s current biosecurity guidance explicitly includes information security, cybersecurity, molecular techniques, and artificial intelligence within biological risk management. (\[who.int\](https://www.who.int/publications/b/69836?utm\_source=openai))  
\#\#\# Organizational containment  
This includes:  
\- Named ownership  
\- Training  
\- Standard operating procedures  
\- Independent review  
\- Incident reporting  
\- Maintenance records  
\- Inventory controls  
\- Approval gates  
\- Change management  
\- Emergency response  
\- Stop-work authority  
The NIH framework assigns responsibilities to investigators, biosafety officers, institutional biosafety committees, and institutions rather than treating safety as the responsibility of a biological part. (\[grants.nih.gov\](https://grants.nih.gov/grants/policy/nihgps/HTML5/section\_4/4.1.27\_research\_involving\_recombinant\_or\_synthetic\_nucleic\_acid\_molecules\_\_including\_human\_gene\_transfer\_research\_.htm?utm\_source=openai))  
\---  
\#\# 5\. Test barrier independence  
Multiple controls are useful only if they do not fail for the same reason.  
For example:  
\- Two kill switches activated by the same environmental signal are not fully independent.  
\- Two genetic dependencies located on the same unstable plasmid may be lost together.  
\- A biological control and its reporter may both fail if expression is silenced.  
\- Two procedural controls performed by the same person during the same step share a human-error pathway.  
The framework should therefore require a \*\*common-cause failure review\*\*.  
For each pair of controls, ask:  
\- Do they depend on the same DNA element?  
\- Do they respond to the same signal?  
\- Do they require the same operator action?  
\- Do they fail under the same environmental condition?  
\- Does one control interfere with the other?  
\- Can a single mutation disable both?  
\- Can one control’s fitness burden select against the entire system?  
A layered design should combine different modalities, such as:  
\\\[  
\\text{Physical containment}  
\+  
\\text{biological dependency}  
\+  
\\text{functional restriction}  
\+  
\\text{procedural oversight}  
\\\]  
This is more robust than stacking several similar genetic circuits.  
\---  
\#\# 6\. Define quantitative assurance claims  
Every containment claim should have an associated metric, method, and acceptance criterion.  
Possible metrics include:  
\- Escape frequency  
\- Survival outside the permitted environment  
\- Mutation frequency  
\- Genetic stability across generations  
\- Construct retention  
\- Time to loss of viability  
\- Recovery after removal of the permitted condition  
\- Growth-rate cost  
\- False activation rate  
\- Failure under environmental rescue conditions  
\- Horizontal-transfer frequency  
\- Decontamination effectiveness  
\- Operator error rate in a simulated procedure  
\- Detection time after a breach  
A generic escape-frequency estimate is:  
\\\[  
f\_{\\mathrm{escape}}  
\=  
\\frac{N\_{\\mathrm{colonies\\ under\\ restrictive\\ conditions}}}  
{N\_{\\mathrm{viable\\ cells\\ tested}}}  
\\\]  
The report must include the assay’s detection limit. If no escape is observed among \\(N\\) tested cells, the correct conclusion is not that escape frequency is zero. A rough upper 95% confidence bound under simple assumptions is:  
\\\[  
f\_{\\mathrm{escape}} \< \\frac{3}{N}  
\\\]  
The exact statistical model should match the experimental design, but the principle is essential: \*\*“not observed” is not equivalent to “impossible.”\*\*  
Every result should include:  
\- Number tested  
\- Number of independent replicates  
\- Detection limit  
\- Confidence interval  
\- Environmental conditions  
\- Duration  
\- Positive and negative controls  
\- Known assay limitations  
This measurement discipline is what turns a containment proposal into an assurance framework.  
\---  
\#\# 7\. Assign evidence maturity  
Every control receives a visible maturity classification.  
\#\#\# Conceptual  
The control has a plausible mechanism but has not been modelled or tested in the project context.  
\#\#\# Literature-supported  
Evidence exists in a related system, but not in the project’s exact chassis, construct, and operating environment.  
\#\#\# In-silico evaluated  
Failure pathways have been modelled, but no direct project data exist.  
\#\#\# Component-validated  
The containment component functions independently.  
\#\#\# System-validated  
The complete containment design has been tested in the intended project context.  
\#\#\# Stress-tested  
The design has been challenged under plausible failure conditions, environmental rescue conditions, mutation pressure, or procedural deviations.  
\#\#\# Independently reproduced  
The performance has been reproduced by another operator, laboratory, or relevant context.  
The report must never present conceptual or literature-supported controls as system-validated.  
\---  
\#\# 8\. Integrate sustainability  
Containment choices can create sustainability tradeoffs.  
For example:  
\- High-temperature decontamination consumes energy.  
\- Large quantities of chemical disinfectant create waste.  
\- Disposable containment materials increase plastic use.  
\- Nutrient dependencies may require expensive supplements.  
\- Continuously expressed kill switches can impose metabolic burden.  
\- Overly complex circuits may increase failure and replacement rates.  
\- Cell-free deployment may reduce ecological persistence but require purified reagents.  
The framework should assess four sustainability dimensions:  
\#\#\# Material burden  
Consumables, plastics, specialized media, and replacement components.  
\#\#\# Energy burden  
Incubation, refrigeration, sterilization, computation, and transport.  
\#\#\# Chemical burden  
Disinfectants, antibiotics, selection agents, solvents, and disposal requirements.  
\#\#\# Biological burden  
Metabolic load, evolutionary instability, waste biomass, and likelihood of failed batches.  
Containment options should be compared using a lifecycle perspective:  
\\\[  
I\_{\\mathrm{total}}  
\=  
I\_{\\mathrm{construction}}  
\+  
I\_{\\mathrm{operation}}  
\+  
I\_{\\mathrm{containment}}  
\+  
I\_{\\mathrm{disposal}}  
\+  
I\_{\\mathrm{failure}}  
\\\]  
The framework should avoid choosing a nominally sustainable biological solution whose containment requirements create a larger total footprint.  
\---  
\#\# 9\. Establish monitoring and change control  
Biocontainment validation is not permanent.  
A new assessment is required if the team changes:  
\- Host organism  
\- Payload  
\- Scaffold size  
\- Vector backbone  
\- Selectable marker  
\- Culture scale  
\- Experimental environment  
\- Product format  
\- Application site  
\- Storage or transport  
\- User population  
\- Software permissions  
\- Containment mechanism  
Each design version should have a \*\*containment passport\*\* recording:  
\- System identity  
\- Intended use  
\- Operating envelope  
\- Consequence pathways  
\- Controls  
\- Evidence maturity  
\- Quantitative results  
\- Residual risks  
\- Reviewer  
\- Approval date  
\- Required reassessment date  
\- Incident history  
\- Decommissioning plan  
ISO 35001 similarly treats biorisk management as an ongoing process of identification, assessment, control, and monitoring rather than a one-time checklist. (\[iso.org\](https://www.iso.org/standard/71293.html?utm\_source=openai))  
\---  
\#\# 10\. Define stop conditions and fallbacks  
A professional framework must specify when development stops.  
Work should pause when:  
\- A critical control fails  
\- Escape exceeds the acceptance threshold  
\- The detection limit is insufficient  
\- A significant consequence pathway lacks an independent barrier  
\- Data provenance is missing  
\- A proposed change exceeds the validated operating envelope  
\- A deployment context lacks regulatory or institutional approval  
\- A software-generated construct fails screening  
\- A responsible reviewer cannot justify proceeding  
Fallbacks should follow a hierarchy:  
1\. Move from living deployment to cell-free operation.    
2\. Move from environmental application to contained application.    
3\. Move from replicating organisms to non-replicating material.    
4\. Remove unnecessary payloads or functions.    
5\. Reduce scale.    
6\. Return to an established host or construct.    
7\. Restrict the system to modelling and laboratory characterization.    
8\. Stop the application entirely if residual risk cannot be justified.    
For ISEF specifically, engineered organisms must not be released or deployed outside the laboratory, and taking products of synthetic biology beyond containment requires prior review under the competition’s current policies.  
\---  
\# Manual for other teams  
A reusable manual should require every team to complete the following sequence.  
\#\# Define  
Describe the system, intended use, environment, scale, user, and end-of-life pathway.  
\#\# Map  
Identify consequence pathways from initiating event to credible harm.  
\#\# Layer  
Assign independent physical, biological, functional, ecological, informational, and organizational controls.  
\#\# Challenge  
Test common-cause failures, mutation, rescue, procedural deviation, and environmental variability.  
\#\# Measure  
Define containment metrics, detection limits, acceptance thresholds, controls, and uncertainty.  
\#\# Classify  
Assign evidence maturity to every containment claim.  
\#\# Compare  
Evaluate containment performance alongside material, energy, chemical, and biological sustainability burdens.  
\#\# Authorize  
Obtain the necessary scientific, biosafety, institutional, and competition review.  
\#\# Monitor  
Track incidents, design changes, control performance, and required reassessment.  
\#\# Decommission  
Define how organisms, constructs, products, records, devices, and waste are safely retired.  
These are workflow verbs rather than another acronym.  
\---  
\# Framework for the sustainability and biocontainment report  
\#\# Opening argument  
Begin by explaining that responsible biotechnology cannot depend on the assumption that one engineered safety part will function perfectly forever. Genetic systems mutate, environmental conditions vary, procedures fail, and applications evolve. Therefore, biocontainment must be treated as a lifecycle-wide assurance problem.  
State the report’s central principle:  
\> \*\*No single containment mechanism is sufficient evidence of safety. Responsible containment requires independent barriers, quantitative validation, lifecycle governance, and a defined response to failure.\*\*  
Explain that the proposed architecture complements established WHO, ISO, NIH, institutional, and ISEF requirements rather than replacing them. (\[iso.org\](https://www.iso.org/standard/71293.html?utm\_source=openai))  
\#\# The inadequacy of single-layer containment  
Discuss why kill switches, auxotrophies, physical containment, or procedural controls can fail individually.  
Explain mutation, metabolic rescue, cross-feeding, fitness costs, operator error, environmental variation, and common-cause failure.  
Avoid presenting any particular technology as universally superior. The appropriate combination depends on the organism, application, environment, and consequence pathway.  
\#\# The proposed architecture  
Introduce the \*\*Lifecycle-Integrated, Evidence-Calibrated, Defense-in-Depth Biocontainment Architecture\*\*.  
Explain its core features:  
\- System boundaries  
\- Intended operating envelope  
\- Consequence pathways  
\- Independent containment layers  
\- Common-cause failure analysis  
\- Quantitative assurance  
\- Evidence maturity  
\- Sustainability assessment  
\- Monitoring and change control  
\- Stop conditions and fallbacks  
\#\# Application to CLASP  
Separate the project into application contexts.  
\#\#\# Laboratory expression  
Assess the host, plasmids, selection markers, proteins, culture scale, storage, transport, waste, and accidental release.  
Controls should prioritize standard physical and procedural containment, appropriate host selection, validated inactivation, inventory control, and institutional review.  
\#\#\# Cell-free diagnostic  
Explain how purified or cell-free operation reduces the risks associated with replication and environmental persistence.  
Still assess reagent safety, sample handling, contamination, product disposal, diagnostic overclaiming, and any human-sample restrictions. Under current ISEF policy, experiments involving humans or human samples require prior review, and testing on humans is prohibited.  
\#\#\# Agricultural concept  
Clearly state that no engineered organism will be environmentally released during the ISEF project.  
Separate laboratory proof of concept from future field deployment.  
Evaluate persistence, horizontal transfer, ecological interactions, reversibility, monitoring, farmer use, distribution, and end-of-life as future requirements—not as solved issues.  
\#\#\# Biomanufacturing  
Evaluate contained production, anaerobic operation where relevant, gas handling, scale-up, equipment integrity, waste, and product separation.  
Do not assume a contained bioreactor eliminates every risk; scale changes the consequences of leakage, equipment failure, and waste generation.  
\#\# Quantitative measurement plan  
Define the measurements used to validate each selected control.  
Include:  
\- Acceptance thresholds  
\- Detection limits  
\- Replicates  
\- Confidence intervals  
\- Positive and negative controls  
\- Stress conditions  
\- Common-cause challenges  
\- Reproducibility between operators  
Emphasize that a containment result must report what could actually have been detected.  
\#\# Sustainability analysis  
Compare containment options across:  
\- Energy  
\- Consumables  
\- Chemical use  
\- Water use  
\- Waste  
\- Transport  
\- Metabolic burden  
\- Expected failure and replacement rates  
Identify tradeoffs honestly. A control that produces less ecological risk but substantially more hazardous waste should not automatically be called sustainable.  
\#\# Governance and accountability  
Define the responsibilities of:  
\- Student researchers  
\- Principal investigator or supervisor  
\- Institutional biosafety body  
\- Laboratory manager  
\- Data/software owners  
\- Future users  
\- External reviewers  
Include approval gates and incident-response responsibilities.  
\#\# Residual risk  
After controls are applied, list what remains uncertain.  
Examples could include:  
\- Environmental behaviour not directly tested  
\- Long-term genetic stability  
\- Cross-feeding  
\- Uncharacterized payload effects  
\- Scale-up uncertainty  
\- Operator variability  
\- Limitations of software screening  
Residual risk should never be hidden merely because the framework has many layers.  
\#\# Fallback hierarchy  
Describe when the team would:  
\- Simplify the organism  
\- Remove a payload  
\- Move to a cell-free system  
\- Reduce scale  
\- increase containment  
\- repeat validation  
\- abandon deployment  
\- stop the project component  
This demonstrates that responsible innovation includes the possibility of deciding not to proceed.  
\#\# Contribution to other teams  
Conclude by publishing reusable materials:  
\- Blank system-boundary worksheet  
\- Consequence-pathway template  
\- Containment-layer catalogue  
\- Common-cause failure checklist  
\- Quantitative assurance worksheet  
\- Evidence-maturity rubric  
\- Sustainability comparison worksheet  
\- Containment passport  
\- Change-control form  
\- Incident and reassessment template  
\- Example completed assessment for CLASP  
The framework becomes useful to the field only if another team can apply it without needing to understand CLASP.  
\---  
\# How to frame its novelty without overclaiming  
Do not write:  
\> “We invented the world’s first comprehensive biocontainment framework.”  
That would be inaccurate because mature biorisk-management frameworks already exist.  
Write:  
\> \*\*We translated established risk-management principles into a modular engineering architecture for synthetic-biology projects, connecting consequence pathways, independent containment layers, quantitative performance claims, evidence maturity, sustainability, and lifecycle change control in one reusable workflow.\*\*  
Your strongest final statement is:  
\> \*\*The framework moves biocontainment from a genetic feature added to a construct into an evidence-calibrated assurance architecture governing the entire biological system, its information, its users, and its lifecycle.\*\*  
That is ambitious, professional, transferable, and defensible.

# Shit that can be put into the payload

**CLASP-Copilot, as currently designed, is primarily an enzyme-scaffold design tool.** Its present models—substrate diffusion, active-site spacing, pathway flux, Michaelis–Menten kinetics, Damköhler numbers, and substrate-capture probability—do **not automatically apply** to CRISPR, kinases, degradation systems, or other payload classes.  
To support payloads beyond enzymes, the software needs a broader **induced-proximity framework**. Each payload pair must be assigned a mechanistic class, with a different objective function and validation model. Proximity can regulate signalling, transcription, chromatin, localization, degradation, folding, and other processes, but each application has distinct geometric and kinetic requirements. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-025-01316-z?utm_source=openai))  
Here is the comprehensive set of payload-pair classes CLASP could theoretically support.

## **1\. Sequential enzyme pairs**

Two or more enzymes catalyse consecutive steps:  
\[  
E\_1:S\\rightarrow I  
\\qquad  
E\_2:I\\rightarrow P  
\]  
The proximity objective is to increase the probability that intermediate (I) reaches (E\_2) before escaping, degrading, or entering a competing reaction.  
This is the **main CLASP payload class** and the one most directly supported by your current mathematics and proposed wet-lab work. Enzyme scaffolding has improved selected pathway outputs, but the benefit depends on enzyme density, pathway kinetics, geometry, and experimental context. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30010058/?utm_source=openai))

## **2\. Enzyme–cofactor-regeneration pairs**

One component performs the main reaction, while the second regenerates a required cofactor.  
The proximity objective is to improve local recycling of factors such as redox carriers, activated donors, or energy-carrying molecules.  
This resembles substrate channeling, but what is transferred or regenerated is a **cofactor**, not necessarily the pathway’s main intermediate.

## 

## **3\. Enzyme–electron-transfer partner pairs**

One payload is a catalytic enzyme and the other transfers electrons to or from it.  
The relevant design objective is:  
\[  
\\text{redox-centre distance}  
\\rightarrow  
\\text{electron-transfer rate}  
\\rightarrow  
\\text{catalytic output}  
\]  
This class needs electron-transfer kinetics and orientation modelling rather than ordinary substrate-channeling equations.

## **4\. Enzyme–substrate-binding or delivery pairs**

One payload captures, concentrates, transports, or presents a substrate. The second payload catalyses its conversion.  
The purpose is not to channel a newly formed intermediate. It is to increase substrate availability near the catalytic component.

## **5\. Kinase–substrate pairs**

One payload is a kinase and the other is its protein substrate.  
Proximity increases the substrate’s effective local concentration around the kinase:  
\[  
K+S  
\\xrightarrow{\\text{recruitment}}  
K:S  
\\xrightarrow{\\text{phosphorylation}}  
K+S\_P  
\]  
The model must account for kinase specificity, substrate orientation, competing phosphatases, and accessibility of the phosphorylation site.

## **6\. Kinase–kinase or receptor-domain pairs**

Two signalling domains are brought together to promote dimerization, trans-phosphorylation, or cooperative activation.  
The objective is not simply minimal distance. The domains must occupy an orientation compatible with activation. Incorrect clustering could create no activity or uncontrolled signalling.

## **7\. Kinase–phosphatase pairs**

A kinase and phosphatase are organized around a common substrate.  
This could control signal amplitude, duration, reversibility, or adaptation. However, bringing antagonistic enzymes together can either improve control or cancel their activities, so the model must include both competing reactions.

## **8\. Protease–substrate pairs**

A protease is recruited close to a specific cleavage target.  
The objective is to increase cleavage probability while minimizing cleavage of unintended proteins:  
\[  
P+T  
\\xrightarrow{\\text{recruitment}}  
P:T  
\\rightarrow  
P+T\_{\\mathrm{cleaved}}  
\]  
This class can implement signal processing, protein activation, inhibition, or circuit switching. Engineered protein circuits have used proteolytic interactions to produce sophisticated signal-processing behaviour. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39666795/?utm_source=openai))

## **9\. Ligase–substrate pairs**

A ligase is recruited to a selected target so that the target receives a covalent modification.  
Depending on the ligase, the modification could alter:

* Protein stability  
* Localization  
* Activity  
* Interaction partners  
* Trafficking  
  This requires modelling modification kinetics and accessibility of the target residue.

## **10\. Degradation-machinery–target pairs**

A target protein is recruited to an E3 ligase, proteasome-associated component, or another degradation system.  
The proximity objective is to induce modification or delivery that causes target destruction:  
\[  
\\text{target}

* \\text{degradation machinery}  
  \\rightarrow  
  \\text{target removal}  
  \]  
  Induced-proximity degradation systems demonstrate that target–effector recruitment can control protein abundance, but productive degradation depends on ternary-complex geometry, accessible modification sites, and the host’s degradation machinery. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-27818-z?utm_source=openai))

## **11\. Deubiquitinase–target or stabilization pairs**

Instead of causing degradation, a payload could remove a degradation-associated modification or otherwise stabilize a target.  
The objective is to extend target lifetime or rescue it from turnover. This is the functional inverse of targeted degradation.

## **12\. CRISPR–regulatory-effector pairs**

One component provides sequence-specific DNA or RNA targeting. The second provides the regulatory function.  
Possible functional classes include:

* Transcriptional activation  
* Transcriptional repression  
* Chromatin modification  
* Epigenetic writing or erasing  
* RNA modification  
* Genome labelling  
  Here the purpose of proximity is to concentrate an effector at a selected nucleic-acid locus. CRISPR scaffold systems have already shown that targeting and regulatory action can be modularized through effector recruitment. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25533786/?utm_source=openai))

## **13\. Split-CRISPR component pairs**

Two inactive CRISPR fragments are recruited together to reconstitute activity conditionally.  
The mechanism is:  
\[  
\\text{inactive fragment A}

* \\text{inactive fragment B}  
  \\xrightarrow{\\text{signal}}  
  \\text{active complex}  
  \]  
  This requires modelling complementation geometry and background assembly rather than substrate channeling. Post-translationally inducible CRISPR architectures have used this general proximity principle. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30633905/?utm_source=openai))

## **14\. DNA-binding-protein–effector pairs**

A DNA-binding component localizes the assembly to a selected sequence, while another payload regulates transcription, chromatin, recombination, repair, or labelling.  
This is broader than CRISPR because the targeting component does not have to be a Cas protein.

## **15\. RNA-binding-protein–effector pairs**

One payload binds a selected RNA, while the second modifies, cleaves, translates, transports, labels, or stabilizes that RNA.  
The purpose is targeted RNA manipulation rather than enzyme channeling.

## **16\. Transcription-factor component pairs**

Two components of a transcriptional regulator are brought together, such as a DNA-recognition component and an activation or repression component.  
Conditional recruitment can turn gene expression on or off without waiting for the regulatory protein itself to be newly produced.

## **17\. Chromatin-writer–reader pairs**

One payload adds a chromatin-associated modification, while another recognizes or propagates it.  
The objective could be local epigenetic regulation, signal amplification, or persistent state formation. This requires locus targeting and chromatin-accessibility modelling.

## **18\. Receptor–signalling-effector pairs**

A receptor or membrane-localized component is paired with an intracellular signalling protein.  
Signal-dependent recruitment could initiate a pathway by placing the signalling effector near the activated receptor or membrane compartment.

## **19\. Adaptor–signalling-protein pairs**

One payload is an adaptor and the other is an effector, enzyme, or regulatory protein.  
The scaffold forms an artificial signalling hub. Natural scaffold proteins already organize enzymes, receptors, ion channels, and signalling components, making this a conceptually valid extension. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30010058/?utm_source=openai))

## **20\. Small-GTPase–regulator pairs**

A molecular switch is paired with a regulator, exchange factor, activating protein, or downstream effector.  
Proximity could control whether the switch is activated, inactivated, or connected to a downstream response.

## **21\. Ion-channel–regulatory-protein pairs**

A channel is recruited near a regulator, sensor, enzyme, or signalling component.  
The relevant benefit is localized regulation or sensing, not intermediate transfer. This generally requires membrane localization and cannot be implemented by a freely diffusing scaffold alone.

## **22\. Transporter–enzyme pairs**

A transporter supplies a molecule, and an enzyme consumes or modifies it near the membrane.  
The proximity objective is to couple transport with immediate conversion and potentially alter the local concentration gradient.

## **23\. Organelle-targeting-component–payload pairs**

One payload localizes to an organelle or membrane compartment, while the second performs a function at that location.  
The scaffold acts as a conditional localization system:  
\[  
\\text{signal}  
\\rightarrow  
\\text{payload recruitment}  
\\rightarrow  
\\text{compartment-specific function}  
\]

## **24\. Cytoskeleton-binding-component–payload pairs**

One component anchors the assembly to actin, microtubules, intermediate filaments, or another structural system. The second payload is thereby localized to a defined cellular region.  
The purpose is spatial control at the cellular scale rather than molecular channeling.

## **25\. Binding-protein–target pairs**

One payload recognizes a molecular target, while the other reports, modifies, captures, or neutralizes it.  
The recognition component could be any sufficiently specific binding domain. The major design variables are affinity, valency, orientation, and specificity.

## **26\. Multivalent recognition pairs**

Two different recognition payloads bind separate features on the same target.  
This can produce coincidence detection or increased avidity:  
\[  
\\text{output}  
\=  
1  
\\quad\\text{only when targets A and B are both present}  
\]  
This could be useful for diagnostics or selective cell recognition, but multivalent binding can also produce nonspecific aggregation.

## **27\. Recognition–reporter pairs**

One payload recognizes a target, while the second produces a detectable signal after recruitment.  
The mechanism is proximity-based reporting, not substrate channeling.

## **28\. Split-reporter pairs**

Two inactive reporter fragments are brought together to restore activity.  
Possible outputs include:

* Luminescence  
* Fluorescence  
* Enzymatic colour production  
* Transcriptional output  
  This is already part of your CLASP architecture through LgBiT and SmBiT.

## **29\. Split-enzyme pairs**

Two inactive fragments of an enzyme are conditionally reassembled.  
The signal controls catalytic activity through complementation rather than by recruiting a complete enzyme to another enzyme.

## **30\. Split-transcription-factor pairs**

A DNA-binding component and an activation or repression component are recruited together.  
The result is signal-dependent gene regulation.

## **31\. Split-protease pairs**

Two inactive protease fragments are brought together to restore cleavage activity.  
This can create a proximity-gated switch or signal-amplification layer.

## **32\. Protein-folding-assistant–client pairs**

A chaperone, foldase, or stabilizing partner is recruited near a client protein.  
The objective is to improve folding, rescue a conformational state, or prevent aggregation.

## **33\. Assembly-factor–structural-protein pairs**

One payload assists the assembly of a larger complex, while the other is a structural component.  
This could control construction of protein cages, filaments, condensates, or other macromolecular structures.

## **34\. Oligomerization-component pairs**

Two or more payloads are recruited to initiate a defined oligomeric state.  
The scaffold controls valency and geometry. The principal risks are uncontrolled polymerization, aggregation, and inter-scaffold crosslinking.

## **35\. Condensate-nucleating pairs**

Payloads promote formation of a biomolecular condensate or localized reaction compartment.  
This is different from a rigid scaffold: the output is a mesoscale phase-separated environment. The model would need phase-separation thermodynamics, concentration thresholds, and valency—not the current substrate-channeling model.

## **36\. Membrane-fusion or vesicle-trafficking pairs**

Two components are brought together to promote membrane docking, fusion, cargo capture, or vesicle trafficking.  
This requires membrane anchoring and strict geometric control.

## **37\. Cargo–motor pairs**

A molecular cargo is recruited to a motor or transport adaptor.  
The purpose is controlled intracellular transport along the cytoskeleton.

## **38\. Cell-surface recognition–effector pairs**

One payload binds a selected extracellular target, while another produces an extracellular, membrane, or intracellular response.  
This could support conditional cell recognition, adhesion, signalling, or effector delivery, but it requires surface-display architecture rather than the current cytosolic scaffold.

## **39\. Protein–nucleic-acid pairs**

A protein payload is paired with a DNA or RNA adaptor, guide, aptamer, or recognition element.  
This can connect programmable nucleic-acid recognition to protein recruitment. It is an adapted CLASP format because one payload is not itself a protein fusion.

## **40\. Covalent-tag–capture pairs**

Two payloads are recruited so that a covalent reaction occurs after proximity.  
Your SpyTag–SpyCatcher locking mechanism belongs to this class. The design objective is to minimize background locking while maximizing signal-dependent capture.

## **41\. Modification-writer–reader pairs**

One payload writes a chemical or post-translational mark, while the second binds the new mark.  
This can create signal amplification, recruitment cascades, or molecular memory.

## **42\. Modification-writer–eraser pairs**

One component adds a modification and another removes it.  
Conditional colocalization can potentially control state transitions, response duration, and reversibility.

## **43\. Competitive inhibitor–target pairs**

A regulatory payload is recruited to inhibit another protein through steric blockade, active-site occupation, or allosteric regulation.  
Here proximity decreases function rather than increasing it.

## **44\. Sequestration pairs**

A target is recruited away from its normal location or interaction partners.  
The output is functional inhibition through localization rather than degradation or chemical modification.

## **45\. Cooperative multi-protein complexes**

Three or more components must assemble to produce a functional complex.  
This includes systems in which:  
\[  
A+B+C\\rightarrow ABC\_{\\mathrm{active}}  
\]  
The software would need to model stoichiometry, assembly order, partial complexes, and combinatorial occupancy.

## **46\. Antagonistic multi-protein systems**

The scaffold organizes an activator and inhibitor around the same target.  
The purpose is to tune thresholds, pulse duration, adaptation, or signal filtering rather than maximize a single reaction.

## **47\. Synthetic protein-logic systems**

Payload interactions can represent logical operations:

* AND: two conditions are required.  
* OR: either interaction produces output.  
* NOT: recruitment inhibits an output.  
* Memory: transient recruitment produces a persistent state.  
* Threshold: output appears only above sufficient occupancy.  
  Protein-level synthetic circuits have demonstrated that reversible binding and irreversible cleavage can be combined to perform complex cellular information processing. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39666795/?utm_source=openai))

## **What CLASP-Copilot should actually support**

The software should define a **payload-pair mechanism field**, such as:

sequential\_catalysis  
cofactor\_regeneration  
electron\_transfer  
kinase\_substrate  
dimerization\_activation  
protease\_cleavage  
targeted\_degradation  
targeted\_localization  
nucleic\_acid\_effector\_recruitment  
split\_component\_reconstitution  
multivalent\_recognition  
covalent\_capture  
sequestration  
multi\_component\_complex

Each class then receives its own model and objective.  
For example:

* Sequential enzymes optimize intermediate capture and pathway flux.  
* Kinase pairs optimize phosphorylation probability and specificity.  
* CRISPR systems optimize locus-localized effector occupancy.  
* Degradation systems optimize productive target–machinery complex formation.  
* Split proteins optimize complementation with low background.  
* Recognition systems optimize avidity and specificity.  
* Covalent systems optimize signal-dependent locking.  
* Localization systems optimize compartment occupancy.  
  The current Copilot should **not claim to predict all these classes quantitatively**. Its calibrated version should initially support sequential enzyme payloads and split-reporter assembly. The others can exist in the software as design categories labelled:  
  **Mechanistically supported extension; quantitative model not yet calibrated.**  
  The accurate broad definition is:  
  **CLASP is a signal-responsive induced-proximity platform. Sequential enzymes are its initial payload class and substrate channeling is its initial functional mechanism. Other payload classes are possible only where bringing defined molecular partners together causes a specific, testable function.**  
  That distinction keeps the platform broad without falsely implying that every protein benefits from being clustered.

# Measurement

\# CLASP Measurement Track    
\#\# \*\*SCALE\*\* — Standardized Calibration, Assembly, and Luminescence Evaluation  
One master workflow. Five stages. Every number is absolute, comparable, and uncertainty-tagged. Built to look intricate and win Best Measurement while staying lean enough for a small team.  
\---  
\#\# The one-line pitch for judges  
\> \*\*SCALE converts every CLASP experiment into SI-traceable, absolute units with full uncertainty budgets, so assembly is measured as molecules per cell — not relative light units.\*\*  
\---  
\# 1\. The SCALE workflow (memorize this)  
| Letter | Stage | What you do | Output |  
|--------|--------|-------------|--------|  
| \*\*S\*\* | \*\*Standardize\*\* | Calibrate instruments and units | RLU → fmol NanoLuc; OD → cells/mL |  
| \*\*C\*\* | \*\*Characterize\*\* | Measure each part alone | Solubility, activity, binding kinetics |  
| \*\*A\*\* | \*\*Assemble\*\* | Measure signal-dependent recruitment | Dose–response, EC50, dynamic range |  
| \*\*L\*\* | \*\*Lock / Link\*\* | Test covalent lock \+ functional output | Retention after EGTA; trehalose fold-change |  
| \*\*E\*\* | \*\*Evaluate\*\* | Uncertainty, reproducibility, model fit | AES ± 95% CI; CV; residual analysis |  
Sub-acronyms under each stage keep the wiki looking dense without adding wet-lab work.  
\---  
\# 2\. Stage S — Standardize    
\#\# Sub-workflow: \*\*UNIT\*\*  
\*\*U\*\* — Units defined    
\*\*N\*\* — NanoLuc standard curve    
\*\*I\*\* — Instrument cross-check    
\*\*T\*\* — Total-cell calibration    
\#\#\# What to do  
1\. \*\*NanoLuc standard curve\*\*    
   Commercial recombinant NanoLuc, serial dilution 0.01–100 fmol \+ furimazine.    
   Fit:    
   \\\[  
   \\mathrm{RLU} \= a \\cdot \[\\mathrm{NanoLuc}\] \+ b  
   \\\]    
   Report \\(a\\), \\(b\\), \\(R^2\\), LOD, LOQ.  
2\. \*\*OD₆₀₀ → cells/mL\*\*    
   ISEF silica-microsphere protocol (or haemocytometer \+ CFU cross-check once).    
   Report conversion factor ± SD.  
3\. \*\*Instrument CV\*\*    
   Same lysate, two plate readers (or two gains on one reader). Target CV \< 15%.  
4\. \*\*Buffer matrix check\*\*    
   Furimazine \+ Ca-EGTA buffers alone → background RLU. Subtract from all later data.  
\#\#\# MVP for S  
\- One NanoLuc curve    
\- One OD→cells curve    
\- One background plate    
\- Written conversion equations in the wiki    
\*\*Software feed:\*\* Dataset \#6 (OD→cells), Dataset \#7 (RLU→fmol).  
\---  
\# 3\. Stage C — Characterize    
\#\# Sub-workflow: \*\*PART\*\*  
\*\*P\*\* — Protein expression & solubility    
\*\*A\*\* — Activity retained after fusion    
\*\*R\*\* — Recruitment pair kinetics    
\*\*T\*\* — Tag / reporter alone    
\#\#\# Designs (minimal set)  
| Construct | Host | Purpose |  
|-----------|------|---------|  
| His6-SpyCatcher | BL21(DE3) | Covalent lock half |  
| SpyTag-sfGFP | BL21(DE3) | Lock \+ visual band |  
| M13-LgBiT | BL21(DE3) | Scaffold reporter half |  
| CaM-SmBiT | BL21(DE3) | Payload reporter half |  
| CaM-mutant-SmBiT (E31A/E104A) | BL21(DE3) | Dead sensor control |  
| sfGFP (no SpyTag) | BL21(DE3) | Negative lock control |  
\*\*Expression host (fixed for all SCALE work):\*\*    
\*E. coli\* BL21(DE3), autoinduction (Overnight Express / ZYM-5052), 18–30 °C overnight. One master expression day → freeze lysates → all later assays from aliquots. Minimizes culture variability.  
\#\#\# What to measure  
1\. \*\*Solubility\*\*    
   Supernatant vs pellet SDS-PAGE → % soluble \= S/(S+P).    
   Target: \>70% for scaffold-like constructs.  
2\. \*\*SpyTag–SpyCatcher kinetics\*\*    
   Mix lysates, stop at 1, 5, 10, 30 min → SDS-PAGE band shift → % covalent complex.    
   Fit pseudo-first-order \\(k\_{\\mathrm{obs}}\\).  
3\. \*\*Split-NanoLuc alone\*\*    
   LgBiT lysate \+ SmBiT lysate ± Ca²⁺ → RLU.    
   Background \= LgBiT alone \+ furimazine.  
4\. \*\*Fusion activity (when enzymes exist)\*\*    
   CaM-OtsA / CaM-OtsB vs untagged → retain \>80% activity (Megazyme / coupled assay).  
\#\#\# MVP for C  
\- Solubility for all four Phase-1 constructs    
\- SpyCatcher gel-shift time course    
\- LgBiT \+ SmBiT ± Ca²⁺ luminescence    
\- One dead-CaM control    
\*\*Software feed:\*\* Datasets \#1 (Spy kinetics), \#2 (solubility).  
\---  
\# 4\. Stage A — Assemble    
\#\# Sub-workflow: \*\*DOSE\*\*  
\*\*D\*\* — Dose–response (Ca²⁺)    
\*\*O\*\* — Occupancy / AES    
\*\*S\*\* — Specificity controls    
\*\*E\*\* — EC50 \+ Hill \+ dynamic range    
\#\#\# Designs  
| Strain / mix | Purpose |  
|--------------|---------|  
| M13-LgBiT \+ CaM-SmBiT | Active assembly |  
| Scrambled-M13-LgBiT \+ CaM-SmBiT | Docking specificity |  
| M13-LgBiT \+ CaM-mutant-SmBiT | Sensor specificity |  
| Free LgBiT \+ free SmBiT | No-scaffold background |  
\*\*Until second backbone exists:\*\* express singly, mix clarified lysates. Same physics, fewer co-transformation failures.  
\#\#\# What to measure  
1\. \*\*Ca²⁺ dose–response\*\*    
   Invitrogen Calcium Calibration Buffer Kit (or MaxChelator-calculated EGTA series):    
   0, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 50, 100 µM free Ca²⁺.    
   Read luminescence every 2 min for 30 min.  
2\. \*\*Fit\*\*    
   \\\[  
   R(C) \= R\_0 \+ \\frac{R\_{\\max}C^{n}}{EC\_{50}^{n}+C^{n}}  
   \\\]    
   Report \\(EC\_{50}\\), \\(n\\), \\(R\_{\\max}/R\_0\\), 95% CIs.  
3\. \*\*Absolute AES\*\*    
   \\\[  
   \\mathrm{AES}  
   \=  
   \\frac{(R-R\_{\\mathrm{blank}})\\cdot\\text{fmol conversion}}  
   {\\text{cells}\\cdot\\text{OD factor}}  
   \\quad  
   \[\\text{assembled NanoLuc molecules per cell}\]  
   \\\]  
4\. \*\*Dynamic range\*\*    
   \\\[  
   \\mathrm{DR} \= \\frac{R\_{\\mathrm{sat}}-R\_0}{R\_0}  
   \\\]    
   Target: \>10-fold.  
\#\#\# MVP for A  
\- Full Ca²⁺ curve for active pair    
\- Two negative controls (scrambled \+ dead CaM)    
\- AES in absolute units    
\- EC50 ± 95% CI    
\*\*Software feed:\*\* Dataset \#3 (dose–response), \#5 (negatives).    
\*\*This is the highest-information experiment — protect it if time slips.\*\*  
\---  
\# 5\. Stage L — Lock / Link    
\#\# Sub-workflow: \*\*HOLD\*\*  
\*\*H\*\* — Hold after chelation (lock test)    
\*\*O\*\* — Output (trehalose)    
\*\*L\*\* — Link geometry series    
\*\*D\*\* — Dual readout (luminescence \+ product)    
\#\#\# Designs (geometry series — your “optimal CTPR” case)  
| Scaffold | Docking pattern | Why |  
|----------|-----------------|-----|  
| CTPR-8 | M13 at 2, 6 | Short / high density |  
| CTPR-11 | M13 at 3, 8 | Mid |  
| CTPR-14 | M13 at 4, 10 | Model-predicted optimum |  
| CTPR-17 | M13 at 5, 12 | Long / lower density |  
| CTPR-14 scrambled | Non-binding | Specificity |  
| CTPR-14 \+ SpyCatcher adjacent | Lock mode | Irreversible |  
If full CTPR library is too heavy, \*\*MVP geometry set \= 3 lengths\*\* (8, 14, 17\) \+ scrambled \+ lock variant.  
\#\#\# What to measure  
1\. \*\*Lock retention\*\*    
   Assemble at saturating Ca²⁺ → add EGTA → re-read RLU.    
   Locked should retain \>80% peak; reversible should drop.  
2\. \*\*Trehalose fold-change\*\* (when OtsA/OtsB ready)    
   Scaffolded vs free enzymes, ± Ca²⁺, Megazyme kit.    
   \\\[  
   \\text{Fold} \= \\frac{\[\\text{trehalose}\]\_{\\mathrm{scaffold,Ca}}}{\[\\text{trehalose}\]\_{\\mathrm{free,Ca}}}  
   \\\]  
3\. \*\*Dual readout\*\*    
   Same lysate: luminescence (assembly) \*\*and\*\* trehalose (function).    
   Plot AES vs product — proves they are separable.  
\#\#\# MVP for L  
\- One lock vs reversible comparison    
\- One trehalose ± scaffold ± Ca²⁺    
\- At least two scaffold lengths if CTPR series exists    
\*\*Software feed:\*\* Dataset \#4 (trehalose fold).  
\---  
\# 6\. Stage E — Evaluate    
\#\# Sub-workflow: \*\*PROOF\*\*  
\*\*P\*\* — Propagate uncertainty    
\*\*R\*\* — Reproducibility (inter-day / inter-operator)    
\*\*O\*\* — Overlay model vs data    
\*\*O\*\* — Outlier and residual checks    
\*\*F\*\* — Final measurement kit / SOP    
\#\#\# What to do  
1\. \*\*Uncertainty budget\*\* for every derived number    
   \\\[  
   u\_c^2(y)  
   \=  
   \\sum\_i  
   \\left(  
   \\frac{\\partial y}{\\partial x\_i}  
   \\right)^2  
   u^2(x\_i)  
   \\\]    
   Sources: RLU noise, OD, protein conc., standard-curve slope, dilution.    
   Report mean ± 95% CI (expanded uncertainty).  
2\. \*\*Reproducibility\*\*    
   \- Same lysate, two days    
   \- Two operators if possible    
   \- Target CV \< 15% for AES at saturating Ca²⁺  
3\. \*\*Model–data overlay\*\*    
   Plot mechanistic ODE (or Hill fit) on top of dose–response with residual plot.    
   Report RMSE and leave-one-point-out error.  
4\. \*\*CLASP Measurement Kit (wiki deliverable)\*\*    
   Lyophilized or frozen aliquots \+ SOP \+ conversion equations \+ example raw plate.    
   Ship concept or share with one collaborating team → inter-lab CV.  
\#\#\# MVP for E  
\- Uncertainty table for EC50 and AES    
\- One inter-day CV    
\- One residual plot    
\- Written SOP \+ raw data deposit    
\---  
\# 7\. Design matrix that looks intricate but is lean  
\*\*Expression host (locked):\*\* BL21(DE3) \+ autoinduction only.    
\*\*Chassis for SCALE:\*\* \*E. coli\* lysates (cell-free readout). Plants / B. subtilis / anaerobic H₂ stay outside the measurement medal track.  
\*\*CTPR series (if you build it):\*\*  
| N | Sites | Role in SCALE |  
|---|-------|----------------|  
| 8 | 2 | Short arm of geometry series |  
| 14 | 2 | Model-predicted centre |  
| 17 | 2 | Long arm |  
| 14 | scrambled | Specificity |  
| 14 | \+ SpyCatcher | Lock |  
\*\*If CTPR not ready:\*\* run SCALE on M13-LgBiT \+ CaM-SmBiT only; geometry series becomes a “planned extension” with modelling already done.  
\*\*Controls (never skip):\*\*  
\- No Ca²⁺    
\- Scrambled docking    
\- Dead CaM    
\- No scaffold    
\- Reporter halves alone    
\- Free enzymes (for trehalose)  
\---  
\# 8\. Absolute metrics you report (medal language)  
1\. \*\*AES\*\* — assembled NanoLuc molecules per cell (or per OD)    
2\. \*\*EC50\*\* — free Ca²⁺ for half-maximal assembly (µM) ± 95% CI    
3\. \*\*Hill n\*\* ± CI    
4\. \*\*Dynamic range\*\* (fold)    
5\. \*\*Lock retention\*\* (% signal after EGTA)    
6\. \*\*Trehalose fold-change\*\* (scaffolded / free) ± CI    
7\. \*\*Solubility %\*\*    
8\. \*\*SpyCatcher conversion %\*\* at 10 min    
9\. \*\*Inter-day CV\*\* of AES    
10\. \*\*Combined standard uncertainty\*\* for every derived quantity    
Every number has: raw data → conversion equation → uncertainty → confidence tier (validated / interpolated).  
\---  
\# 9\. MVP ladder (what “done” looks like)  
| Level | Name | Must have | Medal readiness |  
|-------|------|-----------|-----------------|  
| \*\*M0\*\* | Lights on | NanoLuc curve \+ OD curve \+ one ±Ca²⁺ luminescence | Demo works |  
| \*\*M1\*\* | SCALE core | Full Ca²⁺ dose–response \+ 2 negatives \+ absolute AES \+ EC50±CI | Competitive |  
| \*\*M2\*\* | SCALE complete | \+ Spy kinetics \+ solubility \+ lock test \+ uncertainty budget \+ SOP | Strong Best Measurement |  
| \*\*M3\*\* | SCALE+ | \+ CTPR geometry series (3 lengths) \+ trehalose dual readout \+ inter-day CV | Winning package |  
Do \*\*M1\*\* no matter what. Add \*\*M2\*\* pieces as they finish. \*\*M3\*\* only if CTPR and Ots constructs exist.  
\---  
\# 10\. Software / ORIGAMI hooks (measurement → model)  
| SCALE output | ORIGAMI use |  
|--------------|-------------|  
| NanoLuc \+ OD curves | Unit layer |  
| Spy kinetics | Locking submodel prior |  
| Solubility | Expression penalty |  
| Ca²⁺ dose–response | Primary calibration target |  
| Negatives | Specificity constraint |  
| AES absolute | Training / residual GP target |  
| Trehalose fold | Functional validation, not AES training |  
| Uncertainty | Displayed on every prediction |  
| Geometry series | Tests “14-repeat” hypothesis |  
\---  
\# 11\. Wiki / judging one-pager structure  
\*\*Title:\*\* SCALE — A traceable measurement standard for signal-responsive protein assembly    
\*\*Sections:\*\*  
1\. Why relative RLU is not enough    
2\. UNIT calibration chain    
3\. PART characterization    
4\. DOSE assembly metrology    
5\. HOLD lock and function    
6\. PROOF uncertainty and reproducibility    
7\. Raw data \+ conversion scripts    
8\. Measurement kit / SOP    
9\. How SCALE feeds ORIGAMI    
\*\*Figure set (minimum):\*\*  
\- Standard curves

\---  
\# 12\. Lean rules (so you actually finish)  
1\. \*\*One host, one media, one lysis method\*\* for all SCALE data.    
2\. \*\*One master expression day\*\* → frozen lysates.    
3\. \*\*No purification\*\* until Phase 4 enzyme kinetics (optional).    
4\. \*\*Lysate mixing\*\* until second plasmid backbone exists.    
5\. \*\*Protect the Ca²⁺ dose–response\*\* above all other wet-lab goals.    
6\. \*\*Every plate has blanks, negatives, and a standard.\*\*    
7\. \*\*No orphan numbers\*\* — every value has units, n, and uncertainty.    
8\. \*\*Geometry series is 3 points, not 20.\*\*    
9\. \*\*Trehalose is validation of function, not the definition of assembly.\*\*    
10\. \*\*If time dies, ship M1 \+ uncertainty \+ SOP — that still looks like Best Measurement.\*\*

\#\# Memory card (print this)  
\`\`\`text  
SCALE \= Standardize → Characterize → Assemble → Lock/Link → Evaluate  
UNIT  \= calibrate light and cells  
PART  \= each piece alone  
DOSE  \= Ca²⁺ curve \+ AES  
HOLD  \= lock \+ trehalose
